name: Union of Soviet Socialist Republics

areaKm2.note: LoN Year-Book 1938/39 Table 2: USSR in Europe and Asia 21,176 thousand km2 (pre-1939 frontier). The world_1938 USSR polygon (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aourednik/historical-basemaps/master/geojson/world_1938.geojson) computes to ~21.13M km2. The 1939-40 annexations (Baltic states, eastern Poland, Bessarabia/N. Bukovina, Karelian Isthmus, ~0.45-0.5M km2) were Soviet in June 1941 but lie outside the polygon; high includes them (educated).

population.note: Andreev, Darski and Kharkova demographic balance: 196.7M in June 1941 (incl. territories annexed 1939-40); Rybakovsky's review range 191.8-200.1M (both via the cited page). COW NMC v7 tpop 1941 = 196,659k agrees. The 17 Jan 1939 census (old frontier) gave 170,467k (LoN Year-Book 1938/39 Table 2).

urbanization.note: HYDE via OWID: Russia 1940 = 35.3% urban (high; the USSR as a whole was less urban). Mid ~0.33 matches the 1939 census urban share (~33%, general literature, not fetched). Low = COW upop/tpop 1941 = 32,546/196,659 = 0.165 (cities over 100,000).

activePersonnel.note: Askey (operationbarbarossa.net) total 22 June 1941: 5,448k = Red Army/NKVD/PVO 4,553k + air force 476k + navy 344k + 74,945 construction and civil-department personnel (excluded here). Krivosheev's reconciliation gives 4,902k (low, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II_casualties_of_the_Soviet_Union); some Russian sources give 5.71M (high).

trainedReserves.note: Krivosheev 1997 (Soviet Casualties and Combat Losses, mobilisation section; page not verified): mobilisation decreed 22 June 1941 called the 1905-1918 classes and brought in ~5.3M reservists by 1 July. Harrison 1998 Table 1-5 average 1941 strength 7,100k is consistent. Grade C.

supportPersonnel.note: active minus P roles: air force 476k, navy 344k, plus the army's tank, artillery, engineer, signals, rear services, PVO, fortified-region garrisons and NKVD troops.

mobilizationRatio.note: Krivosheev (via cited page): 4,902k under arms in June 1941 plus 29,575k drafted during the war = ~34.5M served, 0.175 of 196.7M (high). Peak simultaneous strength ~12.2M (Harrison 1998 Table 1-5) on a population reduced by occupation gives the low.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Reconstruction from Askey's 304 divisions (179 rifle): rifle divisions at an average ~8,000-10,000 of the 14,483 wartime establishment, of which ~60-65% in the rifle regiments -> ~5,000-7,500 riflemen x 179. Plus rifle troops of fortified regions excluded (support).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: Mosin rifle, DP LMG, SVT-40 partly issued; shortages of radios, trucks and AT guns

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: army tripled since 1939, many recent conscripts; post-purge junior officers inexperienced

count.note: 19 mountain rifle divisions (Askey) at ~5,000-6,000 infantry each plus 16 airborne brigades (5 airborne corps) at ~3,000.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: as rifle troops, lighter equipment

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: airborne volunteers better trained

count.note: 9 cavalry and 4 mountain cavalry divisions (Askey) at ~6,000-7,000 men each (1941 establishment ~9,200).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: horsed cavalry with light tank and artillery support

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: long-service cavalry tradition, good in forests and marshes

count.note: Askey: 23,295 tanks in the whole USSR on 22 June 1941; 12,842 in the five western districts (sum of district figures). Only ~1,800 T-34/KV; a large share of older T-26/BT needed repair (low ~80% serviceable, educated). Barbarossa article gives ~11,000 frontline (Mercatante; Clark).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: T-34 and KV best tanks of 1941 but ~8% of the fleet; T-26 and BT light tanks obsolescent

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: 29 mechanised corps forming, drivers with a few hours of training, few radios

count.note: Askey: 48,247 artillery pieces 45-305 mm (excl. coastal and railway guns) plus 56,100 mortars 50-120 mm (not counted here). High allows broader counts of guns incl. lighter calibres.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: 76 mm ZiS-3/F-22, 122 mm M-30, 152 mm ML-20 modern and good

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: shortage of tractors, communications and trained FOs

count.note: Batteries. Askey: 8,600 AA guns 25-85 mm; at ~4 heavy guns per battery (light batteries larger) ~2,150 batteries.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: 85 mm 52-K good; light AA scarce

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: PVO crews thinly trained

count.note: Askey: 20,474 combat aircraft in total; fighters ~55-62% of Soviet combat aircraft in 1941 (I-16, I-153, new MiG-3/Yak-1/LaGG-3) - split is an educated reconstruction. Western districts 7,133-9,100 aircraft (Barbarossa article; Glantz).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: mostly I-16 and I-153; ~1,500 modern fighters, few radios

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25. Evidence: pilots averaged few hours in new types; post-purge leadership

count.note: Remainder of Askey's 20,474 combat aircraft: SB, DB-3, TB-3, Su-2, early Il-2 and naval aviation bombers. Educated split.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: SB obsolete; Il-2 and Pe-2 just entering service

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25. Evidence: poor navigation and night training

count.note: Battleships, cruisers and destroyers. Soviet fleets 1941: 3 battleships and 7 cruisers (cited page, note 25) = 10/10/11; plus 59 destroyers (46 modern Gnevny/Soobrazitelny class, cited page). Role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries: destroyers moved from ships_minor.

quality.note: Count-weighted mean (mid counts) of battleships/cruisers 0.3/0.4/0.5 (10) and destroyers 0.45/0.5/0.6 (59), role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries. Rubric rows: quality 0.25-0.5 and 0.5. Evidence: 3 Tsarist-era battleships; Kirov-class cruisers and Gnevny/Soobrazitelny destroyers modern, weak AA and ASW

training.note: Count-weighted mean (mid counts) of battleships/cruisers 0.3/0.4/0.5 (10) and destroyers 0.35/0.4/0.5 (59), role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries. Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: limited sea time, purged command

count.note: 22 patrol vessels (cited page); 269 torpedo boats and 88 minesweepers excluded as coastal craft. The 59 destroyers moved to ships_major (was 59/81/110), role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: modern destroyers, weak AA and ASW

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: limited sea time

count.note: 218 submarines in 1941 (cited page); other counts 212. The largest submarine force in the world, but many small coastal boats and low operational readiness.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: many small M-class; poor torpedoes and sonar

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: low readiness; e.g. only ~35 of 75 Baltic boats operational

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: 1937-38 purges removed most senior commanders; deep-battle doctrine on paper but ad hoc command in June 1941, poor coordination

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.25-0.5. Evidence: national conscript army mid-expansion; mass surrenders in 1941 encirclements, but many units fought on when surrounded (Brest)

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.5-0.75. Evidence: surprise and collapse in summer 1941; existential defence of the homeland raised morale later (high)

weapons.note: Anchor: between 7 (1905) and 8 (1943). Evidence: T-34/KV, ZiS-3, M-30, Katyusha prototypes, SVT-40; most equipment 1930s

armor.note: Anchor: close to 8 (rolled homogeneous armour). Evidence: T-34 sloped armour and KV 75 mm armour best in the world, but only ~1,800 of 23,000 tanks

ships.note: Anchor: between 7 and 8. Evidence: no carriers, Tsarist battleships, large but low-quality submarine force

fortification.note: Anchor: between 7 and 8 (Maginot). Evidence: Stalin Line partly disarmed, Molotov Line incomplete in June 1941

logistics.note: Anchor: between 7 (railways) and 8 (motor transport). Evidence: rail-bound army; 272,600 motor vehicles (Askey) for 304 divisions; broad gauge

communications.note: Anchor: 7 (telegraph, telephone). Evidence: radios scarce below army level, tanks mostly without radios, reliance on landlines

isr.note: Anchor: between 7 (aerial recon) and 8 (radar). Evidence: a few RUS-1/RUS-2 early-warning radars; aerial reconnaissance weak

air.note: Anchor: between 7 and 8. Evidence: I-16/I-153 obsolete; MiG-3, Yak-1, LaGG-3, Il-2, Pe-2 entering service

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 (OWID CSV), 'USSR' series: 1939 = 3,566, 1940 = 3,417 (2011 int$); 1941 not reported. Low allows for the poorer annexed western lands.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Harrison 1998 Table 1-8 (USSR, % of GNP at 1937 factor cost): 17% in 1940, 28% in 1941, 61% in 1942.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: after the Five-Year Plans industry was ~30-40% of GNP; Harrison 1998 stresses the USSR's low-productivity agriculture still employing most workers. (context page: https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/soc/economics/staff/mharrison/public/ww2overview1998.pdf)

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: collectivised agriculture fed the country with little margin (grain exports small after 1933); loss of Ukraine in 1941 turned it into deficit. (context page: https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/soc/economics/staff/mharrison/public/ww2overview1998.pdf)

annualCohort.note: LoN Year-Book 1938/39 Table 3(a), 1926 census: males 20-24 = 6,712k (pop 147M), ~0.91% of population per one-year male cohort; applied to 196.7M gives ~1.8M, reduced because the 1921-23 birth cohorts were thinned by civil war and famine. Reconstruction, grade C.

armor.note: Harrison 1998 Table 1-6 (IVMV): tanks and SPG 4.8k in the last 6 months of 1941 (9.6k annualised, low), 24.4k (1942), 24.1k (1943), 29.0k (1944).

aircraft_fighter.note: Harrison Table 1-6: combat aircraft 21.7k (1942), 29.9k (1943), 33.2k (1944); fighters ~50-55% of Soviet output (educated split).

aircraft_strike.note: Harrison Table 1-6 combat aircraft minus fighters: Il-2 (the most produced aircraft), Pe-2, Il-4, Tu-2.

artillery.note: Harrison Table 1-6: guns 30k in the last 6 months of 1941 (60k annualised), 127k (1942), 130k (1943), 122k (1944); mortars (230k in 1942) excluded.

ships_major.note: Harrison Table 1-6 major naval vessels 62 (1941) falling to 13-23 per year; essentially no capital ships or cruisers were completed after June 1941.

ships_minor.note: Harrison Table 1-6: major naval vessels 62 (1941), 19 (1942), 13 (1943), 23 (1944), minus submarines.

submarines.note: Educated split of Harrison's major naval vessels; ~50 submarines completed 1941-45.

roadKm.note: Educated guess of hard-surfaced roads; the overwhelming majority of Soviet roads were unsurfaced dirt tracks that dissolved in rasputitsa (van Creveld, Supplying War ch. 5).

railKm.note: 106,100 km of railway by 1940 (cited page, incl. annexed lines), up from 81,000 km in 1917; broad 1,524 mm gauge.

majorPorts.note: Leningrad/Kronstadt, Tallinn, Riga, Murmansk, Arkhangelsk, Sevastopol, Odessa, Novorossiysk, Vladivostok; split between four separated fleet areas.

merchantTonnage.note: LoN Year-Book 1938/39 Table 113 (Lloyd's Register, June 1938): U.S.S.R. 1,281k gross tons (excl. Caspian). x1.5 to deadweight (x1.3-1.6); high adds the Baltic states' fleets seized in 1940 (~0.25M GRT, educated).

supplyRangeKm.note: van Creveld ch. 5 (Barbarossa logistics): forces beyond ~300 km from railheads could not be supplied by the motor transport of 1941; the Red Army had only 272,600 vehicles (Askey) and depended on rail.

draftAnimals.note: USSR horse stock 21M in 1940 (Dunn 2005 p. 231, via cited page), down from 34M in 1929; ~11M lost to the German advance 1941-42; the Red Army used 3.5M during the war.

homeDefense.note: 1.3 row: familiar terrain, fortified cities, population support, deep strategic depth and a harsh winter and rasputitsa invaders were not adapted to.

notes: Snapshot date 22 June 1941 (Operation Barbarossa). Population (196.7M), forces, rail and GDP are for the June 1941 USSR INCLUDING the 1939-40 annexations (Baltic states, eastern Poland, Bessarabia, Karelian Isthmus, ~20-23M people), but the requested border hb:1938:USSR is the pre-1939 frontier, so these lands lie outside the polygon; a world_1945 polygon would match better. Mongolia (MPR) not included. Force counts are for the whole USSR (Askey, operationbarbarossa.net); the five western districts held 2,691,674 men, 12,842 tanks, 8,336 combat aircraft and 23,633 guns (sum of Askey's district figures), which a battle agent should use for the frontier battles. P-role personnel are reconstructions from division counts (grade C). Ship convention per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries: battleships, carriers, cruisers and destroyers = ships_major, patrol ships and smaller craft = ships_minor (role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries). Merchant tonnage converted to deadweight at x1.5.
